AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch1: Grouped by whether there is deliberate human intervention: observational studies only record patterns that occur naturally; controlled experiments change only one variable (fair test); in a double-blind trial neither participants nor testers know the group allocation, participants are randomly assigned and handled by an independent administrator, which exposes the placebo effect; surveys, trial and error and case studies are descriptive and cannot establish causation. Exam point: the key to double-blind is both parties unaware plus random assignment.

The skeleton of scientific inquiry: define a testable question, review the literature to avoid repetition, then state a falsifiable hypothesis and prediction, then design and run the experiment, process the data and draw a conclusion, and finally communicate it in a scientific report. Common error: a hypothesis must be able to be disproved by data, not written as proving a conclusion correct; a conclusion applies only to the scope of this study and must not be extrapolated freely.

The independent variable IV is the factor the researcher deliberately changes, the dependent variable DV is the one measured as the result, and controlled variables CV are the other factors that must be kept constant throughout so they do not contaminate the results. Exam point: when writing variables include the measurement method and units (e.g. DV = heart rate per minute); on a graph the IV is always on the x-axis and the DV on the y-axis; a controlled variable is a factor that would otherwise change but is deliberately held fixed.

Validity asks whether the thing that should be measured was measured - too few controlled variables or a systematic error makes it invalid; reliability is whether repeated experiments give consistent results, improved by repeats and replicates; accuracy is how close the data is to the true value, and depends on whether the instrument is calibrated. Key: repeats and replicates can only improve reliability, never accuracy, and this is the most common confusion.

Repeats are the same experiment done over and over by the same person under the same conditions; replicates are several groups run in parallel or a larger number of participants. Measurement error comes from natural variation between subjects and from the measuring process; if it comes from instrument precision, only calibrating the instrument can fix it. Data are often given as a confidence interval, e.g. 45±1.5 means the true value lies between 43.5–46.5 at the 95% confidence level.

Qualitative data contain no numbers (A is taller than B), while quantitative data carry measured values and are further split into discrete (whole numbers only, e.g. number of people) and continuous (any value within a range, e.g. height). Rules for choosing a graph: two continuous variables use a line graph or scatter plot, discrete or category comparisons use a bar chart, proportions use a pie chart. Common error: discrete data must not be joined into a line, and bars on a bar chart must have gaps between them.

Human research requires informed consent, the right to withdraw at any time and protection of privacy; animal work follows the 3Rs - Replacement with alternative methods, Reduction of the number of animals, Refinement of technique to lessen suffering. A risk assessment must state the specific hazard, its risk rating and the matching control measure. Exam point: you must be able to match the three English words of the 3Rs and give one example of each.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch2: Exocrine glands have ducts and release their secretions through a tube onto a surface or into a body cavity (sweat glands, salivary glands, the exocrine part of the pancreas); endocrine glands have no ducts, so hormones pass straight into tissue fluid and then blood, travelling all over the body but acting only on target cells that carry the matching receptor. Common error: the pancreas is both - its exocrine part sends digestive enzymes down the pancreatic duct, while its endocrine part (islets) secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood.

The mnemonic is 4P plus 2TAG: 4P is pituitary, pineal, pancreas and parathyroid, 2TAG is thymus, thyroid, adrenal and gonads, and with the hypothalamus that directs them all this makes nine endocrine glands. Exam point: the adrenal cortex and medulla differ completely in origin, hormones and function and must be learned separately - the cortex secretes cortisol and aldosterone, the medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline.

Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble and derived from cholesterol (cortisol, aldosterone, sex hormones) and can cross the cell membrane, so they are effective taken orally; protein and amine hormones are water-soluble (insulin, growth hormone, adrenaline, ADH), cannot cross the membrane, and are broken down by digestive enzymes if swallowed, so they must be injected. The comparison table must also be filled in with: receptor location, whether a second messenger is used, and speed of onset and duration of action.

Steroid hormones diffuse into the cell, form a hormone-receptor complex with an intracellular receptor and activate genes, which are transcribed into mRNA and translated into protein, changing cell function with a slow onset but long-lasting effect. Protein and amine hormones can only bind membrane receptors and produce the second messenger cAMP, triggering an enzyme cascade: one hormone molecule can activate thousands of molecules, finally producing billions of enzyme molecules, so the onset is fast but short-lived.

The anterior lobe is a true gland: hypothalamic neurosecretory cells send releasing and inhibiting factors into the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system, which stimulates the anterior lobe to secrete TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, GH and prolactin. The posterior lobe is only a storage and release site: ADH and oxytocin are synthesised in the hypothalamus, carried along the axons to the posterior lobe and released directly by nerve impulses. Common error: the posterior lobe does not make its own hormones.

Learn them by source: the hypothalamus makes ADH and oxytocin (released via the posterior lobe); the anterior lobe secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin; the thyroid secretes T3/T4; the adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline and the cortex secretes cortisol and aldosterone; the islet beta cells secrete insulin and alpha cells secrete glucagon. Exam point: TSH and ACTH are trophic hormones.

Most hormones are stabilised by negative feedback: a rise in the target gland hormone in turn inhibits the hypothalamic releasing factor and the pituitary trophic hormone, forming the three-tier hypothalamus to pituitary to target gland loop. A disorder means too much or too little of a hormone, such as hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, diabetes or diabetes insipidus; replacement therapy simply supplies the missing hormone (insulin injection, thyroxine tablets). Positive feedback is rare, the classic example being oxytocin in childbirth.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch3: Information flows one way: dendrites receive, the cell body integrates, the axon conducts, the axon terminal outputs. The myelin sheath is a fatty insulating layer wrapping the axon, formed by Schwann cells in the periphery and oligodendrocytes in the CNS; it prevents current leakage and enables saltatory conduction, and the bare gap between two myelin segments is a node of Ranvier. Exam point: conduction direction is set by the synapse structure and is unrelated to axon length.

Four structural types: multipolar (one axon plus many dendrites, most motor and interneurons), bipolar (one axon plus one dendrite, found in eye, ear and nose), pseudounipolar (a single process that then branches, most sensory neurons) and unipolar (insects only). Three functional types: sensory (receptor to CNS), interneuron (connections within the CNS) and motor (CNS to effector). Common error: pseudounipolar is the one most often examined.

The roughly −70 mV across the membrane is maintained by three factors: (1) the membrane is highly permeable to K⁺ with many leak channels, so K⁺ flows out down its concentration gradient; (2) permeability to Na⁺ is low; (3) large organic anions cannot cross, so negative charge stays inside. The sodium-potassium pump uses 1 ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. Exam point: the pump maintains the concentration gradients, while the resting potential depends mainly on K⁺ leak channels.

A stimulus opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and the inward flow pushes the potential past the −55 mV threshold and up to +30 mV (depolarisation); then Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, and the outward flow brings the potential back down (repolarisation); K⁺ channels close slowly and the excess outward flow causes hyperpolarisation; finally the pump restores the resting state. Common error: depolarisation is Na⁺ in, repolarisation is K⁺ out.

If a stimulus does not reach threshold there is no action potential; once threshold is reached or exceeded the amplitude of the action potential is constant, which is the all-or-none law. A stronger stimulus can only increase the frequency of action potentials, not their amplitude. During the refractory period Na⁺ channels are inactivated and the membrane cannot be excited again, which ensures the impulse travels in one direction and does not turn back. Exam point: if asked what happens when the stimulus is increased, answer frequency rises, amplitude unchanged.

In a myelinated axon ion exchange happens only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the action potential jumps node to node; this is far faster than the point-by-point depolarisation along the whole membrane of an unmyelinated axon and also saves ATP; the thicker the axon and the thicker the myelin, the faster the conduction. Exam point: in multiple sclerosis the myelin is destroyed and conduction slows, showing that myelin insulates and speeds things up rather than generating the potential.

Learn the order: the action potential reaches the axon terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open and Ca²⁺ flows in, synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis, the neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, causing excitation or inhibition. Acetylcholinesterase then breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal. Synaptic transmission is one-way and is also the step most often attacked by drugs and toxins.

A specialised synapse formed between the axon terminal of a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre, with acetylcholine as the neurotransmitter; binding causes the muscle fibre to depolarise and contract. There are four ways of interfering: blocking postsynaptic receptors (curare), inhibiting acetylcholinesterase so transmitter accumulates (organophosphate pesticides), preventing transmitter release (botulinum toxin) and promoting transmitter release (black widow spider venom). Exam point: be able to classify these as acting pre- or postsynaptically.

Receptors are grouped into six types by stimulus: pain nociceptor (tissue damage, ischaemia, excessive pressure and temperature), mechanical (sound waves, pressure, touch), chemical (chemicals, blood pH and gases), thermal (hot and cold), light (eye only) and osmotic osmoreceptor (plasma osmotic pressure, located in the hypothalamus).

All five parts of the reflex arc are essential: the receptor detects the stimulus, the sensory neuron carries it in, the interneuron (in the grey matter of the spinal cord or brain) integrates it, the motor neuron carries it out, and the effector (muscle or gland) responds. The knee-jerk reflex contains only a sensory and a motor neuron (monosynaptic) and is still a reflex. Exam point: a reflex is an unconscious, rapid, automatic response, and answers must state where the interneuron is.

Nervous conduction uses electrical signals and neurotransmitters along fixed point-to-point pathways, is extremely fast (milliseconds), acts briefly and is precisely targeted; endocrine regulation uses hormones carried in the blood, has a slow onset (seconds to hours or longer), acts for a long time and is distributed body-wide but acts only on target cells with receptors. Exam point: both are coordinated by the hypothalamus, and a table comparing speed, duration, mode of transmission and specificity is common.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch4: Three layers of protection from outside in: the skull and vertebral column form the bony casing; the meninges are three layers - dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater; cerebrospinal fluid CSF fills the spaces between the meninges and the ventricles, cushioning against shock, supplying nutrients and maintaining intracranial pressure. Exam point: meningitis is infection of the meninges and a lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid; when answering about protection you must include bone, membranes and fluid.

The frontal lobe handles thinking, planning, voluntary movement and the production of speech; the parietal lobe handles somatic sensation; the temporal lobe handles hearing and language comprehension; the occipital lobe handles vision. The cerebellum controls balance and coordination of movement, making voluntary movement smooth; the medulla oblongata contains the cardiac, respiratory and vasomotor centres and controls reflexes such as swallowing, coughing, sneezing and vomiting; the hypothalamus is the homeostasis centre (temperature, water and salt, feeding, endocrine coordination, autonomic control); the corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres.

The cerebral cortex is divided by function into sensory areas (interpreting impulses from receptors), motor areas (controlling muscles) and association areas (intelligence and emotion). The language areas are almost all in the left hemisphere: Broca's area in the frontal lobe is responsible for producing speech and articulation, and damage means the person cannot speak but can still understand; Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is responsible for language comprehension, and damage means speech is fluent but meaningless and the person cannot understand others.

Grey matter is mainly nerve cell bodies and dendrites, and lies on the surface of the brain (cortex) and in the centre of the spinal cord; white matter is mainly myelinated axons, and lies inside the brain and around the outside of the spinal cord, its colour coming from myelin. Fibre bundles within the CNS are called tracts and fall into three groups: association tracts connect areas of cortex on the same side, commissural tracts connect the two hemispheres, and projection tracts connect the cortex with the brainstem or spinal cord. Exam point: the inner-outer arrangement of grey and white matter is reversed between the brain and the spinal cord.

The PNS connects the CNS with the rest of the body. The afferent (sensory) part brings somatic and visceral sensory information into the CNS; the efferent part splits into two - somatic motor nerves supplying skeletal muscle (voluntary) and autonomic nerves supplying cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands (involuntary), with the autonomic nerves further divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic. Exam point: classification must be set out in two levels, afferent/efferent and then somatic/autonomic, and must not be mixed together.

The sympathetic division works mainly with noradrenaline and dominates under stress: heart rate and contractility increase, blood vessels in skeletal muscle, the heart and the liver dilate while those in the viscera and skin constrict, the pupils dilate, bronchioles widen, digestive activity is inhibited and sweat secretion increases. The parasympathetic division works mainly with acetylcholine and dominates at rest: heart rate slows, pupils constrict, bronchioles narrow and digestion and urination are promoted. Exam point: the two are an antagonistic arrangement in which the same organ receives both sets of fibres.

Facing fear, anger, stress or competition the sympathetic division is activated and the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline, raising cardiac output and blood pressure, increasing blood flow to skeletal muscle, widening the airways, raising blood glucose and increasing sweating, which strengthens and prolongs the response above. Spinal cord cross-section: the dorsal root contains sensory neuron axons and carries the dorsal root ganglion (where the sensory cell bodies are), and the ventral root contains motor neuron axons.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch5: The SRF model links homeostatic mechanisms into one chain: stimulus (deviation from the set point), detection by a receptor, control centre (usually the hypothalamus or medulla), response by an effector, feedback. Negative feedback cancels the change and returns the body to the set point and is the mechanism for most hormones and for temperature regulation; positive feedback amplifies the change, as with oxytocin in childbirth and the clotting cascade. Exam point: receptor, control centre and effector must all be written.

Do not reverse the directions: glycogenesis = glucose to glycogen, glycogenolysis = glycogen to glucose (liver and muscle); gluconeogenesis = fat/protein to glucose (liver); lipogenesis = glucose to fat (liver); lipolysis = fat to fatty acids (liver).

The beta cells of the islets secrete insulin, the only hormone in the body that lowers blood glucose, promoting glycogenesis, lipogenesis and glucose uptake by cells; the alpha cells of the islets secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (rapidly raising glucose under stress) and the adrenal cortex secretes cortisol (promoting glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipolysis). Exam point: insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood glucose.

The liver is central: when blood glucose is high it stores glucose as glycogen or converts it to fat; when blood glucose is low it breaks down glycogen and, through gluconeogenesis, converts fat and amino acids into glucose, and can also reuse lactate produced by muscle. Skeletal muscle can only store and break down its own glycogen for its own use and cannot release glucose back into the blood. Adipose tissue stores fat under the action of insulin and breaks fat down for energy under the action of glucagon and adrenaline.

Type 1 diabetes is caused by destruction of the beta cells and an absolute lack of insulin, is more common in younger patients and requires insulin injection; type 2 is caused by fewer receptors or a reduced response in target cells (insulin resistance), is mostly linked to obesity and age, and can first be managed with diet, exercise and oral drugs. Exam point: read the blood glucose curve - a diabetic has a higher fasting glucose and a higher peak after eating that falls more slowly; glucose in the urine shows the renal threshold has been exceeded.

Separate heat loss from heat production: metabolic heat production (a by-product of cellular respiration) is the only route that actually produces heat; radiation (emitting heat to the surroundings), conduction (exchanging heat with objects in direct contact), convection (moving air or water continually carrying heat away from the skin surface), evaporation (sweat vaporising and carrying away a large amount of heat) and excretion (passing warm urine and faeces and exhaling warm air) can only lose heat.

When too hot, skin arterioles dilate so more blood flows to the surface and loses heat by radiation and convection, while sweat glands secrete more and lose heat by evaporation. When too cold, skin blood vessels constrict to reduce blood flow to the surface, skeletal muscles contract involuntarily and shiver to produce heat, arrector pili muscles contract to give goose bumps, thyroxine and adrenaline raise the metabolic rate, and behavioural responses appear such as putting on clothes, curling up and finding somewhere warm. Exam point: shivering produces heat, goose bumps produce almost none.

Hypothermia means the core body temperature is too low, so enzyme reactions and metabolism slow down and in severe cases there is loss of consciousness and irregular heartbeat. Heat exhaustion is usually caused by heavy sweating during intense exercise plus vasodilation, leading to dehydration and a fall in blood volume, with dizziness, weakness, cold clammy skin and low blood pressure; heat stroke is the complete failure of temperature regulation, with a very high core temperature, dry hot skin with no sweating and impaired consciousness, and can be fatal. Exam point: distinguish the two by sweating and skin condition.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch6: Body fluids are divided into intracellular fluid and extracellular fluid, and extracellular fluid includes plasma, tissue fluid and also lymph, cerebrospinal fluid and others. Extracellular fluid is the true internal environment of the cells, and its composition and osmotic pressure must stay stable. Exam point: substances moving between the blood and cells must cross two barriers, the capillary wall and the cell membrane; the main difference between plasma and tissue fluid is that plasma contains more plasma proteins.

The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney and consists of the renal corpuscle and the renal tubule: the glomerulus is a ball of capillaries wrapped by Bowman's capsule, and together these are the renal corpuscle where filtration occurs; after that come the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle (which dips into the medulla and helps concentrate urine) and the distal convoluted tubule, which finally joins the collecting duct. Exam point: a diagram is often given to label each section and to ask which part is regulated by ADH or aldosterone.

Filtration occurs at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: high pressure forces water, glucose, amino acids, salts and small waste molecules into the capsule, while blood cells and plasma proteins are held back. Reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule, returning useful substances and water to the blood. Secretion is the active transfer of excess substances from the blood into the tubule. Finally the urine leaves via the collecting duct, ureter, bladder and urethra. Urinalysis for glucose, protein, blood cells and pH can indicate kidney disease or diabetes.

Water loss raises plasma osmotic pressure, which excites osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, so the posterior lobe releases ADH, which acts on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, increasing aquaporin water channels so more water is reabsorbed, giving a small amount of concentrated urine, and also causes thirst. Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal cortex, acts at the same site and promotes Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ excretion, with water following osmotically. With plenty of water ADH falls and urine is dilute and plentiful.

O₂ is carried mainly bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells, with a small amount dissolved in plasma; most CO₂ is carried in plasma as hydrogencarbonate, with a small amount bound to haemoglobin. CO₂ and water form carbonic acid catalysed by carbonic anhydrase, which dissociates to release H⁺, so a rise in CO₂ lowers pH. Carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate form a buffer pair that keeps blood pH at about 7.35–7.45.

Two classes of receptor: the central chemoreceptors in the medulla are sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺, while the peripheral receptors in the aortic and carotid bodies are sensitive to O₂, CO₂ and pH. The control centre is the respiratory centre in the medulla, with an inspiratory and an expiratory area. The effectors are the diaphragm (phrenic nerve) and the intercostal muscles (intercostal nerves). Exam point: CO₂ is the strongest stimulus for breathing, and O₂ only matters when it falls very low.

Rapid deep breathing blows off too much CO₂, raising blood pH and weakening the breathing drive. Hyperventilating before a dive seems to let you hold your breath longer, but not because you carry more oxygen - it is because the signal of rising CO₂ that drives the urge to breathe is lost, so the person loses consciousness from cerebral hypoxia before even feeling the need to breathe. When used to relieve anxiety, watch for dizziness, tingling in the hands and feet and other signs of respiratory alkalosis.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch7: Learn them by structure and size: viruses are the smallest and are non-cellular, and must parasitise living cells; bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes that can reproduce independently; fungi are eukaryotes, often with hyphae and spores; parasites include protozoa and helminths, all eukaryotic with complex life cycles. Exam point: antibiotics work only on bacteria and not on viruses, fungi or parasites, a high-frequency short-answer question.

Bacteria are prokaryotes: no membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, but they have a cell wall, circular DNA and plasmids, and reproduce by binary fission. Shapes are cocci, bacilli, spirilla and vibrio. Gram stain steps are crystal violet primary stain, iodine mordant, alcohol decolouriser, safranin counterstain; Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall and stain purple, Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer with an outer lipopolysaccharide layer and stain red.

A virus has only a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) and a protein coat called the capsid, and some also have an envelope; it has no cell structure and no ribosomes, cannot metabolise or reproduce on its own and must use the host cell's machinery to replicate, so it is regarded as lying between non-living and living. Three differences from bacteria: non-cellular rather than a prokaryotic cell, cannot reproduce independently whereas bacteria divide by binary fission, and antibiotics do not work on viruses but do work on bacteria.

These can be grouped into contact and non-contact: direct contact (touching, kissing), indirect contact (shared towels, utensils and other fomites), body fluid transmission (blood and sexual contact), vector transmission (mosquitoes and other carriers, e.g. malaria), contaminated food and water (faecal-oral route), and airborne droplets and aerosols. Exam point: prevention measures must match the specific route - for the vector route, for example, control and repel mosquitoes.

The first line of defence includes skin (sebum and sweat inhibit microbes), mucous membranes, nasal hairs and cilia (sweeping mucus towards the pharynx), stomach acid and acidic vaginal secretions, lysozyme in tears and saliva, earwax and the flushing action of urination. The four protective reflexes each have a stimulus and a response: sneezing (irritation of the nasal mucosa), coughing (irritation of the lower respiratory tract), vomiting (overdistension of the stomach or toxins) and diarrhoea (increased peristalsis after intestinal irritation flushes the irritant away).

The second line of defence is not specific to a particular pathogen: phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) engulf and digest pathogens; damaged tissue releases histamine and other substances that dilate local blood vessels and increase permeability, producing redness, swelling, heat and pain and recruiting more phagocytes; pyrogens raise the hypothalamic set point and cause fever, which inhibits pathogen reproduction and speeds up the immune response; the lymphatic system filters tissue fluid and carries pathogens to lymph nodes.

Once activated by antigen, B cells proliferate and differentiate into plasma cells and memory cells, and plasma cells secrete antibodies. Six antibody actions: neutralising bacterial toxins or enzymes so they are inactivated, binding the surface of viruses to stop them entering cells, coating bacteria so phagocytes can engulf them, agglutinating bacteria, viruses or foreign blood cells, lysing pathogens (destroying their membrane), and reacting with soluble substances to make them insoluble so they can be phagocytosed. Memory cells make the secondary response faster and stronger.

T cells mature in the thymus and target intracellular pathogens, cancer cells and transplanted tissue. Helper T cells recognise antigen presentation and release cytokines, activating cytotoxic T cells and B cells; cytotoxic T cells use perforin to punch holes in the target cell membrane and release granzymes, triggering apoptosis. Comparison: B cells use antibodies against extracellular pathogens while T cells kill intracellular pathogens by direct contact, and both produce memory cells.

Classified by the source of antibody and whether the body makes it: natural active = acquired after illness; natural passive = the baby receives maternal antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk; artificial active = vaccination, in which the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells with long-lasting protection; artificial passive = injection of antitoxin or immunoglobulin, which acts immediately but gives no memory cells and only short-lived protection. Herd immunity needs a high enough proportion of people immune to block transmission.

Antibiotics act only on bacteria: by action they are bacteriostatic (inhibiting reproduction) or bactericidal, and by range broad-spectrum (affecting many bacteria, easily disrupting normal flora) or narrow-spectrum; antiviral drugs instead have to interfere with the virus entering the cell or replicating. Resistance arises from random mutation plus selection: too low a dose, an incomplete course or overuse leaves resistant bacteria behind to multiply. So the full dose and full course must be taken as prescribed, and antibiotics do not work on viral infections such as the common cold.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U3 · Ch8: Each of the three tools has its job: restriction endonucleases recognise a specific sequence and cut the DNA, staggered cuts giving sticky ends and straight cuts giving blunt ends; the plasmid is the vector and must be cut with the same enzyme to produce complementary sticky ends; DNA ligase seals the gaps in the sugar-phosphate backbone, joining the gene of interest to the plasmid to form a recombinant plasmid, which is then put into bacteria to be amplified. Exam point: complementary sticky ends are the key, which is why both steps must use the same enzyme.

Bacteria are first treated with CaCl₂ to increase the permeability of the cell wall and membrane and make them competent, then the recombinant plasmid is added and a short heat shock drives the DNA into the cells, which are then grown in LB medium to multiply. Because the plasmid carries a resistance gene, on medium containing antibiotic only bacteria that were successfully transformed survive and form colonies, completing the selection. Exam point: antibiotic selection picks out the bacteria that have taken up the plasmid; it is not about killing all the bacteria.

Gene therapy introduces a normal gene into cells to replace a faulty one, and is mostly used for single-gene recessive disorders (cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia, Huntington's disease), but it cannot repair severe organ damage that has already occurred. Cell replacement therapy uses stem cells induced to differentiate into healthy cells (such as neurons) which are then transplanted, to treat Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. Tissue engineering goes further, seeding stem cells onto a scaffold to grow three-dimensional tissue or organs.

Diabetes is treated with recombinant human insulin or insulin analogues; hyperthyroidism is treated with drugs, radioactive iodine or surgery to suppress or remove the thyroid, while hypothyroidism is treated by replacing thyroxine. Alzheimer's and Parkinson's are neurodegenerative diseases, and conventional drugs only relieve symptoms, so using healthy neurons differentiated from stem cells for cell replacement is now being explored. Exam point: be able to distinguish the two approaches of replacing what is missing and swapping out bad cells.

Insert the human insulin gene into a plasmid, put it into bacteria or yeast, let them express it in large amounts and then extract and purify it to obtain a synthetic hormone - high yield, high purity, no reliance on animal pancreases, and it also avoids animal-borne pathogens and immune rejection. Vaccines can be produced the same way as subunit vaccines (taking only one antigenic protein from the pathogen), which is safer than traditional attenuated or inactivated vaccines. Exam point: rDNA products are proteins made using cells as factories.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U4 · Ch9: Genetic information flows DNA to (transcription) mRNA to (translation) protein: mRNA is transcribed from DNA in the nucleus following complementary base pairing, then goes to the ribosome where every three bases (a codon) correspond to one amino acid as it is translated into a polypeptide. Genes control characteristics by controlling protein synthesis. Exam point: a mutation that changes a codon but not the amino acid is a silent mutation.

Gene mutations affect only one gene and may be point mutations (base substitution) or frameshift mutations (insertion or deletion that throws the reading frame out completely); chromosome mutations affect many genes or a whole length of chromosome, such as deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation and aneuploidy (caused by non-disjunction). Mutagens such as radiation and certain chemicals raise the mutation rate. Mutations are random and undirected, yet they are the ultimate source of new alleles.

Random orientation of homologous chromosomes into gametes during meiosis (independent assortment) and crossing over between homologous chromosomes, together with the new alleles provided by mutation and random fertilisation, all create the variety of gene combinations in the offspring. Non-disjunction is the failure of a pair of chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis, giving gametes with an abnormal chromosome number (e.g. trisomy 21). Exam point: only mutation produces new alleles; the rest merely recombine them.

The gene pool is the sum of all the alleles in a population, can be described by allele frequencies, and is used to compare populations of the same species at different times or places. Allele frequencies are dynamic and are affected by mutation, selection pressure, random genetic drift (including the founder effect) and gene flow. Exam point: evolution is defined as the change in allele frequencies in a population's gene pool from generation to generation - individuals do not evolve, populations do.

Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations as individuals migrate, and it reduces differences between populations; random genetic drift is chance fluctuation in allele frequencies in small populations, unrelated to whether they are adapted, and the founder effect is a special case (a few individuals found a new population whose gene pool is not representative); natural selection is directional, with selection pressure leaving more offspring from individuals with favourable phenotypes. Exam point: the effect of drift gets stronger as the population gets smaller.

Speciation requires reproductive isolation first: a geographical barrier interrupts gene flow and the separated gene pools change independently under natural selection and drift until they can no longer interbreed. Sickle cell anaemia is the classic case: in malarial regions heterozygotes (sickle cell trait) resist malaria and have a survival advantage over both normal homozygotes and affected homozygotes, so the disease allele is kept at a high frequency, which is called heterozygote advantage.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U4 · Ch10: A specific DNA fragment is amplified in large amounts in vitro, each round having three steps: high temperature denaturation separates the double strands, cooling anneals the primers to the complementary sequences, and heating extends them as Taq polymerase synthesises a new strand from the primer. Taq comes from a thermophilic bacterium and can withstand high temperatures without denaturing, so the cycle can be repeated and the amount of product about doubles each round, growing exponentially. Exam point: the order must be denaturation, annealing, extension.

DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the positive electrode in an electric field; the gel acts as a molecular sieve so shorter fragments travel further, separating DNA by length, and the banding pattern is a DNA fingerprint that can be used for paternity testing, forensics and species comparison. Sanger sequencing adds chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides to the reaction so strand synthesis stops at random, and the sequence is then read off by length. Exam point: PCR amplifies, electrophoresis separates.

Comparative genomics studies and compares the genome sequences of different species to find shared and differing genes; comparative proteins compare the amino acid sequence differences of the same protein between species. The smaller the differences, the closer the relationship and the shorter the time since divergence. Bioinformatics uses computers and statistical tools to handle these huge sequence data sets and to build and correct phylogenetic trees. Exam point: both kinds of evidence rely on the amount of difference being proportional to the time since divergence.

All three are molecular-level evidence: endogenous retroviruses are fragments of ancient viruses inserted into the human genome that no longer move out again, and the same insertion position shows a common ancestor; mitochondrial Eve is the most recent common maternal ancestor of modern humans traced from mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited only through the mother; DNA hybridisation measures similarity by how well DNA from different species re-pairs after being separated into single strands. All three give consistent conclusions.

A phylogenetic tree uses branching to show common ancestors and the order of divergence between species: if two species branch at the same most recent common ancestor they are the closest relatives; the closer a branching point is to the present, the later the divergence; branch length can also show the amount of change. Exam point: you only need to read the diagram, judging which species are most closely related, which diverged first, and whether a trait is a shared derived character or convergent evolution; you are not required to draw one.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U4 · Ch11: A fossil forms when the remains, traces or impressions of an organism are replaced by minerals or preserved in sedimentary rock. The conditions are demanding: rapid burial, hard parts (bone, shell, teeth) and no decomposition or disturbance. The fossil record is therefore incomplete and represents only a small part of the biodiversity of the time; soft-bodied organisms, terrestrial organisms and those in forest environments are especially unlikely to leave fossils.

Relative dating only establishes order, not an absolute age. Stratigraphy uses the principle that in sedimentary rock the lower layers are older and the upper younger, together with the relationships of superposition and cross-cutting; index fossils are fossils with a short time range, wide geographical distribution, high numbers and easy identification, and they allow rock layers at different places to be correlated so the relative age of fossil-bearing layers can be worked out. Exam point: the key features of an index fossil are a short time range plus a wide distribution.

Radiometric dating relies on the constant rate of isotope decay and uses half-lives to calculate absolute ages. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years; the carbon-14 in an organism is fixed at death and the ratio to carbon-12 then falls with decay, making it suitable for organic remains up to tens of thousands of years old; potassium-argon dating measures the decay of potassium-40 to argon in volcanic rock, with a half-life of about 1.25 billion years, and works for rocks millions to billions of years old but not for sedimentary rock itself.

The geological timeline places fossils into eras, periods and epochs using the results of relative and absolute dating. You must be able to use the timeline to decide which period a fossil belongs to, and to read off the order of divergence and degree of relatedness from a phylogenetic tree. Exam point: the two are often combined in a question - first decide from the tree who is more closely related, then use the dates to state when they diverged; note that appearing earlier does not mean more primitive, nor does it mean being the ancestor.

Vestigial organs are structures that are still present but clearly reduced and no longer serve their original function, such as the human appendix, coccyx, wisdom teeth and ear muscles; they suggest that ancestors once needed these structures and therefore support evolution. Comparative anatomy compares homologous structures (same structure, function may differ, such as the human arm and the whale flipper); comparative biochemistry compares DNA and protein sequences, and the smaller the differences the closer the relationship.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U4 · Ch12: Humans belong to the order Primates, family Hominidae, along with the great apes (orangutan, gorilla, chimpanzee); humans did not evolve from modern apes but share a common ancestor with them. Differences between species within Hominidae ultimately come from differences in DNA nucleotide sequences, and the smaller the sequence difference the closer the relationship and the later the divergence. Exam point: the closest living relative of humans is the chimpanzee; the DNA sequence difference is very small, yet they are still different species.

Four distinguishing dimensions within Hominidae: relative size of the cerebral cortex (largest in humans, linked to intelligence and language), mobility of fingers and toes (the human thumb is opposable, specialised for a precision grip, while ape thumbs are shorter), posture and locomotion (humans are bipedal while apes mainly brachiate), and jaw projection and dentition (the human jaw does not project, canines are small and the dental arch is parabolic, while apes have a markedly protruding mid-face and large canines).

The three forms of locomotion match different anatomical adaptations: bipeds have the foramen magnum centred at the base of the skull, an S-shaped spine, a broad short bowl-shaped pelvis, inward-angled femurs forming a carrying angle, and a foot with an arch and a non-opposable big toe; brachiators have extremely mobile shoulder joints, long powerful arms and knuckle-walking hooks; quadrupeds have limbs of nearly equal length, a foramen magnum towards the back and a narrow long pelvis. Exam point: the position of the foramen magnum is the key to identifying bipedalism.

Australopithecus afarensis and africanus were gracile, with a small brain capacity but already bipedal, afarensis being earlier (about 3.2 million years ago) with a more projecting face. Paranthropus robustus was heavily built, with a sagittal crest on the skull roof for powerful chewing muscles and large flat molars, adapted to chewing tough plants; it was a specialised vegetarian side branch, not a direct ancestor of modern humans.

The overall trend is a gradual increase in brain capacity and a more flattened, straight jaw: Australopithecus about 500 mL; Homo habilis between that and Homo erectus, the earliest member of our genus to make stone tools; Homo erectus about 1000 cm³, using fire and making Acheulian hand axes; Neanderthals up to 1350–1400 mL, with heavy brow ridges and a projecting occiput, large-brained but not a direct ancestor of modern humans; Homo sapiens with a flat face and high forehead.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/HBY 人体生物学/U4 · Ch13: Timeline: about 5–6 million years ago the hominins diverged from the apes; Australopithecus (afarensis about 3.2 million years ago) was already bipedal; Homo habilis made the earliest stone tools; Homo erectus appeared about 1.8 million years ago, left Africa and used fire; Neanderthals were distributed across Eurasia about 100 000 years ago; Homo sapiens then spread worldwide. Key African fossil sites include Hadar, Olduvai Gorge and the South African cave sites.

Tool culture went from simple to complex: Homo habilis had Oldowan stone tools, simply knocking a few flakes off a pebble to make a chopper; Homo erectus moved into the Acheulian culture, making hand axes worked on both faces and symmetrical in shape and using fire; Neanderthals had the Mousterian culture, using a prepared core technique to strike regular flakes. Exam point: match species to tool culture.

Besides stone tools there is a series of other cultural evidence: Homo erectus began to use fire (controlling it and cooking food); Neanderthals left signs of burying the dead and caring for the injured and sick; Homo sapiens produced cave paintings, carvings and other art and ornaments; language and symbolic ability appeared with the development of brain capacity and the prefrontal cortex; agriculture was a much later invention that moved humans from hunting and gathering to a settled life and changed their own diet and range of diseases.

Humans used fire, clothing, shelter, medicine and agriculture to change their own environment and so weakened the original selection pressures: clothing and shelter against the cold reduced the advantage of body hair and cold-tolerant body shape; medicine and vaccines meant the alleles for many fatal diseases were no longer strongly eliminated; agriculture brought a new diet and new diseases, and also brought new adaptations such as lactose tolerance. The result is that selection pressures have become human-made, changing both their direction and their speed.
